why: 2026-09-20: a reply said 'no open work is blocking either way' in its own next-steps bullet and then closed with "Don't archive this session" -- the two cannot both be true, and nothing caught it before the person did. The advisory require_one_of above only checks that ONE of the two fixed sentences is present; it has no way to notice that the reply also asserts the opposite of the one it picked. Unlike the archive verdict itself -- deliberately left a judgment call, per the-boildown's own Install section, because no script can tell a real reason from a content-free recap -- a reply is never allowed to assert both halves of the same contradiction at once, whatever the real state is, so this one is blocking rather than advisory. Narrow on purpose: it does not try to verify the verdict is CORRECT, only that the reply does not talk itself out of its own answer. Second incident, same day: a reply's own Boildown bullet said "PR #165 merged... -- nothing left to do there" (scoped to that one closed PR) and correctly closed with "Don't archive this session" because an unrelated question was still open elsewhere -- the flat match had no notion of scope, so a per-item "nothing left to do" read identically to a whole-session one. Fixed by excluding an immediately-following scope qualifier (there / on it,that,this / for it,that,this) from both patterns in this entry, same family as the double-quote-citation exemption above it: a phrase scoped away from the whole session is not asserting the opposite of the verdict, any more than a quoted citation is. Third, 2026-09-28: "The six updater fixes are still waiting upstream" -- work handed to another repository's queue, true beside "You can archive this session" -- was refused the same way, so 'upstream' and 'in/on another repo' joined the still-phrase's scope list. Work waiting in someone else's repository is not this session's outstanding work.

why: 2026-09-22: a reply reported its own eight commits pushed, said "You can archive this session", and left six unpushed commits sitting in a source clone in the same container -- which archiving releases. Morgan, same day (strength: decided): "if changes are done locally but not pushed to main or precedent-beta-v01 then never never recommend 'You can archive this session' (unless the work is intended to be lost!) - this is very important". The mechanism is tools/precedent_container_safe.py, which scans every git checkout in the container -- this repo, its siblings, the home directory's clones, and whatever the source config declares -- for uncommitted changes, untracked files, and commits no remote can reach. Blocking rather than advisory, unlike the archive sentence itself above: the verdict stays a judgment call, but 'would anything be lost' is a fact about a filesystem, and releasing the container is the one closing claim that cannot be taken back next turn. An engine with no copy of the scanner reports nothing and blocks nothing, the same way an unknown predicate does.

unless_reply_declares_loss.why:
2026-09-23: the rule's own `why` above has always carried Morgan's parenthesis -- "(unless the work is intended to be lost!)" -- and the code never implemented it. The refusal even told the reader to "say in the reply that it is meant to be lost" and then ignored them doing so. A session said exactly that in three consecutive replies about 34 superseded watermark commits in a clone 74 behind its origin, on an owner the git proxy refuses pushes to; all three were refused, so all three closed by telling Morgan not to archive a session he could safely archive. A gate that forces a false statement is no longer a safety mechanism. The escape is not a password: _declares_loss also requires the reply to NAME every unsafe checkout, so the 2026-09-22 case that built this rule -- a session that had never looked at the clone holding six unpushed commits -- is still caught, because it could not have named it.

2026-09-23, later the same day: the phrase list itself turned out to be the next version of the same bug. A different session had ALREADY said the substance plainly -- 'safe to let the container reclaim them', 'confirmed superseded... busywork' -- across two replies about the same kind of dead watermark commits, and both were refused for matching none of the four fixed strings, so a session that had done the work of establishing loss was safe still could not say so without guessing the exact incantation. Morgan: "That rule, as you read it, it makes no sense... if there's some way to force it to fire, that would be great." A phrase LIST was never going to close this gap; the fix is a structured marker (`**Checkout disposition:** NAME -- discard (reason)`) checked per unsafe checkout by name, same shape as park-it's own `**Disposition:**` line, so the escape is legible and greppable rather than a password to guess. The phrase list stays as a fallback for prose that already reads correctly under the old rule; the marker is what a reply should reach for going forward.

why: 2026-10-19, Morgan (strength: decided): "if your session is following a multi-step plan. You cannot tell me to archive it unless the plan is fully complete Or I explicitly tell you that I am finishing the plan early." A session following a plan names it on a `**Plan:**` line in its Boildown; tools/precedent_reply_check.py reads that plan's `- [ ]` checklist from disk and refuses the archive sentence while a box is unticked. Two escapes: the person's own word, quoted on a `**Plan ended early:**` line; or the plan handed to another session that get_session confirms is running with it, linked on a `**Plan handed to:**` line (Morgan, 2026-10-19, strength: decided). It reads only a plan the reply names and that keeps a checklist; anything else is the-boildown's blocker 5 in prose. An engine without this branch reports it as unknown and blocks nothing.

why: 2026-10-01: two prompts a session wrote told another session to land work, though the person had not said to. fence-block-for-paste passed both, because it checks that a block says where it goes, not what it authorizes. 2026-10-08: it refused a block that ended at the feature branch, because the block's situation paragraph reported that a tool had told an earlier session to open a pull request to main; in a block that says it stops at the feature branch, a clause narrating what a session or tool did or was told is not an instruction, and every other clause is still judged. Later on 2026-10-08: the rule skipped any line with 'no' or 'without' in it, so 'Merge it into main, no questions asked' passed; a negator now exempts a clause only when it governs the landing verb, and the rule reads the other ways a block says land (make it live, ship it, merge the PR, gh pr merge, git push origin main). Morgan: 'shouldn't it understand the intent behind commands not just the literal words?' (practice: read-for-intent). 2026-10-20, found fixing the ladder set's copy: any quoted span holding push, merge or land counted as the approval, so a refusal quoted further down ("push refused") granted landing; the quote now counts only when it opens with the person's approval or order, and a tool's quoted output is blanked before the approval is looked for. And a landing noun with no verb addressed to the reader ("A push to main runs the deep check") was read as an order: every verb-led trigger now counts its verb only where it is addressed (a clause start, or after then, so, you, can, must, to and the like), and skips a non-final item of a bracketed list of examples, as the ladder set's copy does. Commands (gh pr merge, --base main, git push naming main) stay orders wherever they stand.
